claim: Emotional responsiveness in neonates, particularly their ability to discern vocal emotions, plays an evolutionarily adaptive role in human communication and adaptive behaviors.
source: Emotional responsiveness in neonates, particularly their ability to discern vocal emotions, plays an evolutionarily adaptive role in human communication and adaptive behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the adaptive role of emotional responsiveness, drawing from established understanding in the field.

claim: The study involved 120 healthy neonates categorized into six groups based on their gestational age ranging from 35 to 40 weeks.
source: In a study involving 120 healthy neonates categorized into six groups based on their GA (ranging from 35 and 40 weeks), we explored their emotional responses to vocal stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the current study.

claim: The assessments occurred during natural sleep states using the odd-ball paradigm and event-related potentials.
source: The assessments occurred during natural sleep states using the odd-ball paradigm and event-related potentials.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: A distinct developmental change occurs at 37 weeks gestational age, marking the point at which neonates exhibit heightened perceptual acuity for emotional vocal expressions.
source: The results reveal a distinct developmental change at 37 weeks GA, marking the point at which neonates exhibit heightened perceptual acuity for emotional vocal expressions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The heightened perceptual acuity for emotional vocal expressions at 37 weeks GA is substantiated by the presence of the mismatch response, akin to an initial form of adult mismatch negativity, elicited in response to positive emotional vocal prosody.
source: This newfound ability is substantiated by the presence of the mismatch response, akin to an initial form of adult mismatch negativity, elicited in response to positive emotional vocal prosody.
evidence: This describes the neurophysiological evidence (MMR) supporting the main finding from the study's data.

claim: No discrimination of emotional vocal expressions is observed in acoustically matched control sounds.
source: Notably, this perceptual shift's specificity becomes evident when no such discrimination is observed in acoustically matched control sounds.
evidence: This is a finding from the control condition in the experimental data.

claim: Neonates born before 37 weeks gestational age do not display discrimination ability for emotional vocal expressions.
source: Neonates born before 37 weeks GA do not display this level of discrimination ability.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing different GA groups.

claim: The current data are not yet robust enough to fully support the application of neonatal MMR as a screening tool for autism.
source: Moreover, while these findings introduce the potential for a valuable screening tool for conditions like autism, characterized by atypical social-emotional functions, it is important to note that the current data are not yet robust enough to fully support this application.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement by the authors about the limitations of their current findings for clinical application.

claim: The human brain has evolved to possess a heightened sensitivity to the emotional expressions of others.
source: Over the course of evolution, the human brain has evolved to possess a heightened sensitivity to the emotional expressions of others (Lindquist et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Human infants exhibit a remarkable ability to discern vocal emotions even prior to the full maturation of their visual system.
source: Remarkably, even prior to the full maturation of their visual system, human infants exhibit a remarkable ability to discern vocal emotions (Blasi et al., 2011; Soderstrom et al., 2017; Vaish and Striano, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Prosodic elements of speech, including pitch, intensity, and rhythm, function as universal and non-linguistic channels for emotional communication.
source: Prosodic elements of speech, including pitch, intensity, and rhythm, function as universal and non-linguistic channels for emotional communication (Latinus and Belin, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Infants who have not yet acquired language exhibit differentiated responses to emotional prosody conveying happiness, fear, anger, and sadness within the age range of 2–12 months.
source: Numerous studies have established that infants, including those who have not yet acquired language, exhibit differentiated responses to emotional prosody conveying happiness, fear, anger, and sadness within the age range of 2–12 months (e.g. Caron et al., 1988; Fernald, 1993; Graham et al., 2013; Grossmann et al., 2010; Singh et al., 2002; Walker-Andrews and Grolnick, 1983; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: During the neonatal period, compelling evidence points to the presence of emotion-specific responses to emotional cues conveyed through vocal prosody.
source: More specifically, during the very early stages of postnatal life, often termed the neonatal period (encompassing infants under four weeks of age), compelling evidence points to the presence of emotion-specific responses to emotional cues conveyed through vocal prosody.
evidence: This statement is supported by the subsequent mention of various measurement methods and studies.

claim: Emotion-specific responses to vocal prosody in neonates have been identified through assessments of eye-opening scores.
source: These responses have been identified through various measurement methods, including assessments of eye-opening scores (Mastropieri and Turkewitz, 1999), event-related potentials (Cheng et al., 2012), and near-infrared spectroscopy (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Emotion-specific responses to vocal prosody in neonates have been identified through event-related potentials.
source: These responses have been identified through various measurement methods, including assessments of eye-opening scores (Mastropieri and Turkewitz, 1999), event-related potentials (Cheng et al., 2012), and near-infrared spectroscopy (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Emotion-specific responses to vocal prosody in neonates have been identified through near-infrared spectroscopy.
source: These responses have been identified through various measurement methods, including assessments of eye-opening scores (Mastropieri and Turkewitz, 1999), event-related potentials (Cheng et al., 2012), and near-infrared spectroscopy (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Prior research has primarily focused on the perception and discrimination of emotions among traditionally defined term neonates, treating them as a homogenous cohort.
source: However, prior research has primarily focused on the perception and discrimination of emotions among traditionally defined term neonates, a group that includes infants born within a five-week span (37–41 weeks) of GA, treating them as a homogenous cohort.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature, based on the authors' review.

claim: No study has explored emotion processing in neonates with varying gestational ages prior to this research.
source: Surprisingly, to date, no study has explored emotion processing in neonates with varying GAs.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in the literature based on the authors' review.

claim: The discovery of the developmental milestone for emotional sensitivity provides valuable insights for early diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism.
source: The discovery of this developmental milestone not only advances our understanding of the cognitive mechanisms underlying human social-emotional functioning but also provides valuable insights for early diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism (Jones et al., 2014; Molnar-Szakacs et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement combines the current finding with cited research on autism to suggest potential clinical implications.

claim: MMN is an auditory ERP component that demonstrates a negative shift in response to deviant sounds when compared to standard sounds.
source: MMN is an auditory ERP component that demonstrates a negative shift in response to deviant sounds when compared to standard sounds (Näätänen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a definition of MMN supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: MMN can be elicited without requiring the subject's attention, making it particularly suitable for recording in young infants.
source: Importantly, it can be elicited without requiring the subject's attention, making it particularly suitable for recording in young infants (Cheour et al., 1998; Cheour et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement about MMN properties is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In neonates, the MMN ERP component often manifests as a positive response rather than the traditional MMN.
source: It is worth noting that in neonates, this ERP component often manifests as a positive response rather than the traditional MMN (e.g. Cheng et al., 2012; Chládková et al., 2021; Kostilainen et al., 2020; Richard et al., 2022; Thiede et al., 2019; Virtala et al., 2022; Winkler et al., 2003; Winkler et al., 2009), leading many researchers to refer to it as the mismatch response (MMR) in the neonatal brain.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The selection of positive emotions over negative ones was guided by ethical considerations and previous research indicating an early preference for positive emotions in neonates.
source: Our selection of positive emotions over negative ones (e.g. fear, sadness, or anger) was guided not only by ethical considerations but also by previous research indicating an early preference for positive emotions in neonates (Farroni et al., 2007; Mastropieri and Turkewitz, 1999; Zhang et al., 2019; with the exception of Cheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This explains the methodological choice based on ethics and cited previous research.

claim: The MMR was extracted using ERP difference waves, computed by subtracting the ERP evoked by the standard stimulus from the ERP evoked by the deviant stimulus.
source: The MMR was extracted using ERP difference waves, computed by subtracting the ERP evoked by the standard stimulus (neutral sound) from the ERP evoked by the deviant stimulus (happy sound) (Näätänen et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: Brain electrical activity was recorded from the F3, F4, C3, C4, P3, and P4 sites following the international 10/20 system.
source: Brain electrical activity was recorded from the F3, F4, C3, C4, P3, and P4 sites following the international 10/20 system.
evidence: This describes the electrode placement methodology in the study.

claim: The neonatal MMR exhibits a frontal distribution.
source: However, this study primarily focused on data from electrodes F3 and F4, as the neonatal MMR exhibits a frontal distribution (Cheng et al., 2012; Cheour et al., 2002).

claim: MMR amplitudes were smaller in the GA35 and GA36 groups compared to the GA37, GA38, GA39, and GA40 groups.
source: In general, MMR amplitudes were smaller in the GA35 (0.590 ± 4.579 μV) and GA36 (0.141 ± 4.807 μV) groups compared to the GA37 (2.801 ± 5.585 μV), GA38 (2.760 ± 4.382 μV), GA39 (3.401 ± 4.871 μV), and GA40 groups (3.311 ± 5.491 μV).

claim: No significant differences in MMR amplitudes were found in pairwise comparisons after Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons.
source: However, no significant differences were found in pairwise comparisons after Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons.

claim: The MMRs evoked by vocal stimuli were smaller in the GA35 group compared to GA37, GA38, GA39, and GA40 groups.

evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons.

claim: The MMRs evoked by vocal stimuli were smaller in the GA36 group compared to GA37, GA38, GA39, and GA40 groups.

claim: The identification of the 37 week GA mark aligns with previous research, which indicated emotional sensitivity in term neonates born at or after 37 weeks of gestation.
source: Our identification of the 37 week GA mark aligns with previous research, which indicated emotional sensitivity in term neonates born at or after 37 weeks of gestation (Cheng et al., 2012; Farroni et al., 2007; Mastropieri and Turkewitz, 1999; Zhang et al., 2019) and in preterm neonates (GA <37 weeks) tested at term age (Kostilainen et al., 2020).

claim: The ten disyllables were standardized to have the same mean intensity and had duration of 400ms.
source: These ten disyllables were then standardized to have the same mean intensity and had duration of 400ms using Adobe Audition (v.2022; Adobe Systems Inc, San Jose, CA).
evidence: This describes the stimulus processing methodology.

claim: The fundamental frequency (f0) alone does not convey emotional content in voices.
source: We hypothesized that the fundamental frequency (f0) alone does not convey emotional content in voices and that neonates require multiple other prosodic cues embedded in the high-frequent component to discern emotions, as suggested by Cheng et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited previous research.

claim: Neonates require multiple prosodic cues embedded in the high-frequent component to discern emotions.
source: We hypothesized that the fundamental frequency (f0) alone does not convey emotional content in voices and that neonates require multiple other prosodic cues embedded in the high-frequent component to discern emotions, as suggested by Cheng et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited previous research.

claim: Ten nonvocal sounds were generated to match the f0 contours and temporal envelopes of their corresponding vocal sounds.
source: As a result, ten nonvocal sounds were generated to match the f0 contours and temporal envelopes of their corresponding vocal sounds.
evidence: This describes the control stimulus creation methodology.

claim: The sound stimuli were presented in two blocks: the vocal and nonvocal conditions, utilizing the odd-ball paradigm.
source: The sound stimuli were presented in two blocks: the vocal and nonvocal conditions, utilizing the odd-ball paradigm.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each block consisted of 240 standard stimuli (80%) and 60 deviant stimuli (20%).
source: Each block consisted of 240 standard stimuli (80%) and 60 deviant stimuli (20%).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each sound had a duration of 400 ms, and the inter-trial interval was silent, with varying durations ranging from 500 to 700 ms.
source: Each sound had a duration of 400 ms, and the inter-trial interval was silent, with varying durations ranging from 500 to 700 ms.
evidence: This describes the experimental timing parameters.

claim: Each block lasted for 5 min, with a 5 min break separating the two blocks, resulting in a total EEG recording duration of 15 min.
source: Each block lasted for 5 min, and the order of the vocal and nonvocal blocks was counterbalanced across participants. A 5 min break separated the two blocks, resulting in a total EEG recording duration of 15 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental duration and design.

claim: Auditory stimuli were presented at a sound pressure level of 55–60 dB, with an average background noise intensity level of 30 dB.
source: Auditory stimuli were presented through a pair of loudspeakers positioned approximately 30 cm away from the neonates' left and right ears, at a sound pressure level of 55–60 dB, with an average background noise intensity level of 30 dB.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and acoustic parameters.

claim: Brain electrical activity was recorded using an electrical amplifier at a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz.
source: We recorded brain electrical activity using an electrical amplifier (NeuSen.W32, Neuracle, Changzhou, China) at a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz.
evidence: This describes the data recording methodology.

claim: The data were recorded online with reference to the left mastoid and subsequently re-referenced offline to the average of the left and right mastoids.
source: Initially, the data were recorded online with reference to the left mastoid and subsequently re-referenced offline to the average of the left and right mastoids.
evidence: This describes the EEG referencing methodology.

claim: Electrode impedances were meticulously maintained below 10 kΩ throughout the recording process.
source: Throughout the recording process, electrode impedances were meticulously maintained below 10 kΩ.
evidence: This describes the data quality control procedure.

claim: Ocular artifacts were eliminated from the EEG data using a regression procedure implemented in NeuroScan software.
source: We eliminated ocular artifacts from the EEG data using a regression procedure implemented in NeuroScan software (Scan 4.3, NeuroScan, Herndon, VA).
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methodology.

claim: The EOG-corrected EEG data were offline filtered with a half-amplitude cutoff range of 0.01–30 Hz.
source: The EOG-corrected EEG data were then offline filtered with a half-amplitude cutoff range of 0.01–30 Hz and segmented from 200 ms before sound presentation until 1000 ms after sound onset.
evidence: This describes the data filtering methodology.

claim: Epochs were baseline-corrected relative to the mean voltage during the 200 ms preceding sound presentation.
source: Epochs were baseline-corrected relative to the mean voltage during the 200 ms preceding sound presentation.
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing methodology.

claim: Any epochs containing artifacts with peak deflections exceeding ± 200 μV were rejected.
source: Any epochs containing artifacts with peak deflections exceeding ± 200 μV were rejected (see also Biro et al., 2021; Di Lorenzo et al., 2021; Kumaravel et al., 2022), followed by averaging for each experimental condition.
evidence: This describes the artifact rejection criteria, supported by citations to similar methodologies.

claim: The time window for the MMR component was pre-defined as 150–400 ms after sound onset.
source: The time window for the MMR component was pre-defined as 150–400 ms after sound onset, based on prior knowledge (Cheour et al., 2002), and utilized throughout the data analysis.
evidence: This describes the analysis time window selection, based on cited previous research.

claim: The number of valid epochs did not exhibit a significant difference across neonatal groups.
source: The number of valid epochs did not exhibit a significant difference across neonatal groups.
evidence: This is a result from the data quality analysis.

claim: Figure 1 displays MMR waveforms recorded from all six electrodes.
source: Figure 1 displays MMR waveforms recorded from all six electrodes.
evidence: This references the visual data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Figure 3 presents oscillograms and spectrograms of the auditory stimuli utilized in this study.
source: Oscillograms and spectrograms of the auditory stimuli utilized in this study are presented in Figure 3, generated using Praat (v.6.3.17, https://www.praat.org).
evidence: This references the visual data presented in Figure 3.
